2.3 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the sharp shortfall in allocation of 
the Ministry as compared to the projected demand, despite its repeated recommendation 
for increasing the budgetary allocation of the Ministry, keeping in view the scope, reach 
and value AYUSH can add to the health of the people. Given its indigenous/traditional 
element, cost effectiveness and a safe alternative to modern system of medicine, the 
Ministry of AYUSH, through its schemes and strategies, can help  AYUSH system of 
healthcare to emerge as a valuable system of medicine in healthcare delivery. The 
Committee, therefore, is of the view that budgetary constraints should not be allowed to act 
as a stumbling block to achieve the mission objective s to positi on AYUSH system as the 
primary and preferred system of healthcare in India. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that adequate budgetary support be provided to the Ministry as and when 
required by it.

ii. Under skill development in AYUSH sector component, as per the approved EFC note, it

2.10 The Committee expresses it concern over shortfall in the allocation of funds to 
Ministry of AYUSH in both the Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes. The 
reason behind lower allocation could b e the fact that PM Vrikshayush has not been 
approved yet.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should address 
all the administrative exigencies and complete all the ground work including indentifying 
land for planting of medicinal plant s etc, before the newly conceptualized PM Vrikshayush 
Yojana is approved. Preparatory exercises beforehand will give the scheme much needed 
head start and will significantly help in achieving the desired objectives of the scheme. The 
Committee, however, expects the Ministry of Finance to provide adequate fund for Central 
Sector Scheme at R.E. stage. 
2.11 The Committee is anguished to note shortfall of funds for NAM.  The Committee 
apprehends that the components of NAM aiming to strengthen AYUSH facilities including 
AYUSH hospitals, HWCs, dispensaries, institutions, Drug Testing labs, pharmacies etc 
would be severely affected. The Committee, is of the view that a vital scheme like NAM 
should not be made to suffer due to shortage of fund s and therefore required funds may be 
allocated at the RE stage.

SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY  
NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM) 
3.1 The National AYUSH Mission is a flagship Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Ministry 
which was launched in September, 2014 and was approved originally for continuation till March, 
2021. The Ministry of AYUSH is proposing for continuation of NAM from 1.04.20 1 to 
31.03.2026 for consideration of EFC of Department of Expenditure.  
 
3.2 NAM envisages better access to AYUSH services through AYUSH Hospitals and 
Dispensaries, mainstreaming of AYUSH through co -location of AYUSH facilities at Primary 
Health Centres (P HCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs) and 
ensuring availability of AYUSH drugs and trained manpower. It also aims to improve the quality 
of AYUSH Education through enhancement in the number of upgraded educational Institutions,  
sustained availability of Quality Raw materials and improved availability of quality Ayurveda, 
Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy (ASU &H) drugs through increase in number of Pharmacies 
and setting up of Drug Testing Laboratories in the States.  
 
3.3 The Natio nal Health Policy (NHP) 2017 has advocated mainstreaming the potential of 
AYUSH systems within a pluralistic system of Integrative healthcare. Accordingly, i n 
convergence with National Health Mission (NHM), a total of 27495 AYUSH doctors (11741 
AYUSH docto r under co -located facilities and 15754 AYUSH doctor under Rashtriya Bal 
Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) have been deployed under NHM as on 30.06.2020.  
 
3.4 A comparative analysis of BE & RE 2020 -21 and projected demand BE allocation for 
2021-22 for NAM shows that an allocation of Rs. 705.00 crore was made in BE 2020 -21 which 
was reduced to Rs. 400.00 crore at the RE stage.  An allocation of Rs. 553.80 crore has been 
made in BE 2021-22 against the projected requirement of Rs.775.00 crores.

3.5 The Committee finds that variations between BE & RE allocation is not limited only 
to the year 2020 -21 only but it has been there even in the previous years.  As is evident 
from the Table 17, as against the Expenditure Finance Commission approval of Rs. 800 
crore and Rs. 1000 crore for the year 2018 -19 and 2019 -20 respectively, an amount of Rs. 
504.43 crore and Rs. 506.60 crore were actually allocated.  The Committee finds it quite 
strange that the BE allocation in the year 2019 -20 was reduced by almost 50 percent at RE 
stage.  The Committee takes a very serious view on this phenomenon and recommends that 
such a practice needs to be discouraged as it makes a mockery of the budgetary provision.  
3.6 To a specific query about the reasons for variation in the BE & RE allocation for 2020-21 
the Ministry has submitted that as per the guidelines issued by Department of Expenditure (DoE) 
on dated 04.05.2020, only 50% grant of approved Central Share was released to respective 
States/UTs for the approved activities of AYUSH HWCs and other activities of NAM. Due to 
present pandemic situation of COVID -19, only few States/UTs were able to withdraw the fund 
from treasury to their State AYUSH Society with matching State Share. Further, for 
implementation of other activities of NAM, Grants-in-aid were released to only those States/UTs 
who have reported expenditure as well as submitted UCs at least upto 75% and also assured to 
utilize the remaining amount at the earliest.  
3.7 The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation of Rs. 553.80 crore for 2021-22 is 
less by Rs. 151.20 crore a s compared to the BE of 2020 -21.  The Committee feels that this 
reduction in allocation could be due to under utilization of allocated fund for the last year. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to 
fully utilize the budgetary allocation made this year so as to justify its claim for higher fund 
allocation. The Committee notes that only Rs. 553.80 crore has been allocated for NAM in 
2021-22 against the projected requirement of Rs. 775.00 crores.  The Committee ta king 
cognizance of various vital components under NAM believes that NAM needs to be given 
adequate budgetary support.  This Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Ministry has the 
capacity to increase the outreach of AYUSH healthcare services to different parts  of the 
country including rural and remote areas and also strengthen AYUSH infrastructure with 
respect to institutions drug testing labs, etc. Keeping in view a target of setting up of 3100 
HWCs in 2021 -22, the Committee recommends the Ministry to assess i ts financial 
requirements realistically and approach Ministry of Finance to enhance the fund at the RE 
stage.

NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD (NMPB) 
3.20 National Medicinal Plants Board was set up vide resolution notified on 24th November, 
2000 headed by Union Minister of Health & Family Welfare. At present, the Board is headed by 
Hon’ble Minister of AYUSH with Secretaries of various Departments as ex-officio members and 
nominated members representing various fields. The Board was reconstituted on 01st August, 
2018 and the first meeting of the reconstituted Board was held on 30th August, 2018.  
 
3.21 The NMPB envisages to tap the potential and comparative advantage of India in the 
medicinal plants sector so that it can realize its potential of Global Leadership in this field by 
comprehensive development of conservation, cultivation, collection, processing, marketing, 
research and extension support system for the sector. 
 
3.22 NMPB is currently implementing the Central Sector Scheme in “Conservation, 
Development and Sustainable Management of Medicinal Plants”. Financial assistance is 
provided under the scheme for development of Medicinal Plants (MPs) Sector. 
 
3.23 Major Components of the Scheme include: 
 
a) In-situ conservation, In-situ resource augmentation, Ex-situ Conservation; 
b) Engaging Eco Task Force for rehabilitation of critical Medicinal Plant Habitats: 
c) Support to Joint Forest Management Committees (JFMCs) / Panchayats / Van 
Panchayats / Self Help Groups (SHGs) / (BMCs); 
d) Research, Technology Development and Quality Assurance; 
e) Marketing Intervention; 
f) Awareness Building, Exposure v isits, Education and Capacity Building of 
Stakeholders through Information, Education and Communication 
g) (IEC) strategy; 
h) Promotion of Herbal Gardens, Home Herbal Gardens, School Herbal Gardens, 
Institutional and Public Herbal Gardens; 
i) Establishment of Regio nal-cum-Facilitation Centres (RCFCs) of NMPB; and 
implementing agencies of NMPB throughout the country.

finds the utilization trend of NMPB satisfactory for the year 2019 -20.  The Committee is of 
the view that our country with rich bio -diversity has traditionally been a hub of precious

public health system.  For optimum use of these resources, the need of the hour is to make 
available financial as well as other resources for successful implementation of the scheme. 
The Committee is of the view that NMPB should get the soil tested for specific plantation so 
the income of the farmer may be enhanced through medicinal plantation. The Committee 
would like to emphasize on the enhancement of allocation for NMPB so that the various 
components envisaged under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme is focused upon and 
promoted.

Ministry should take up the matter of pending UCs with States particularly those having 
high number of pending UCs on an urgent basis and encourage them to clear the pending 
UCs.

for Assessment of AYUSH Marke t Size (FAAMS) at the National Medicinal Plants Board and 
through the “Invest India” team. COVID -19 has created 4 -6 times increase in the export of raw 
material and/or extracts of at least 5-6 herbs from India to various countries. Major importers are 
US, UK and Europe. In the first 6 months of 2020, Asvagandha has become No.3 in the list of 
top selling herbs / herbal products in US. In India also there is 400-600% growth in the immunity 
products like Chyawanprash. Herbal ingredients like Giloi, Tulsi, Ging er, Turmeric etc., are in 
the main list as per demand. Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH are encouraging Organic 
Cultivation as one of the means to promote the exports. With the help of Forum on India 
Traditional Medicine (FITM) / Research and Informa tion System for Developing Countries 
(RIS), Ministry of AYUSH is exercising to introduce new HS Code system for export of herbal 
drugs / extracts etc.

material as well as finished products. Cultivation of medicinal plants will provide the source 
document for the raw material which is a major requirement in many countries for the import of

3.33 The Committee notes that while  India is second to China in the herbal trade, China 
is having 6 times more business on herbs/herbal products as compared to India.  The

international trade has established Foru m for Assessment of AYUSH Market Size

need to be focused upon.

3.44 The Committee is anguished to note that the proposal for creation of 24 posts is yet 
not approved.  The Committee, time and again, has been laying emphasis on having 
adequate manpower for the Board so that it could effectively implement the mandate 
assigned to it.  This laid back approach of the Ministry is not in sync w ith its objective 
mission of giving impetus to the cultivation, conservation and documentation of medicinal 
plants. The Committee is of the view that in the absence of adequate manpower the dream 
of achieving the objective cannot be realized  and it, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
accord priority to the human resource requirement of the Board as it is the nodal agency

received from State Medicinal Plants Boards (SMPBs), out of four regular posts sanctioned by

SMPBs.  Apart from Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, there is no separate regular

plants cannot function alone without the active support of SMPBs. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Ministry that issue of shortage of manpower in SMPBs 
should be taken up with the States/UTs and t hey may be convinced of the importance of

minimum number of manpower required in a SMPB be laid down clearly so that the 
SMPB understand the need to give the support to the NMPB as well as involve itself fully in 
the promotion of the medicinal plants of that State. The Committee strongly believes that 
the schemes of medicinal plant can not be implemented properly till a robust structure in 
the States (SMPBs) with adequate f unds and full time manpower is made available.  The 

30 
 
Committee, therefore, exhorts the Ministry to persuade the States/UTs to have separate full 
time manpower for SMPBs for better operational efficacy.

3.49 The Committee is appreciative of the achievements of the Ministry, however, it feels 
that a lot more needs to be done in this area.  The Committee has been emphatically 
pursuing the issue of quality control and scientific validation of AYUSH drugs.  The 
Committee, however, expresses concerns over the reported presence of metals in AYUSH 
drug formulations and safety of these medicines.  Instances of side -effects of AYUSH 
medicines and other products have also come to light.  The Committee believes that a solid 
and robust quality control mechanism is the only way to ensure credibility and safety of 

32 
 
AYUSH drugs. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that in order to have scientific 
validation, more and more clinical trials need to be done to fill up the gap due to lack of 
evidence based medicines.  Given the growing popularity of AYUSH systems, it is the need 
of the hour to lay utmost focus  on scientific validation and strong documentation.  The role 
of Central Drug Controller becomes very important in approval of drugs which have 
undergone pre -clinical trials, clinical trials etc.  The Committee, further, believes that 
publication of peer-reviewed papers in reputed international journals will go a long way in 
establishing the credibility and authenticity of AYUSH systems of medicine.  The 
Committee is also of the view that there should be separate and adequate funding for 
clinical trials and  scientific research which should stand international scrutiny so that 
AYUSH drug get the global recognition and acceptability.

PHARMACOVIGILANCE INITIATIVES FOR ASU&H DRUGS 
3.55 During the formative stage of the Pharmacovigilance initiative for ASU& H Drugs since 
implementation of the Central Sector Scheme in December 2017, three-tier network  of 
Pharmacovigilance centres has been established comprising of a National Pharmacovigilance 
Coordination Centre (All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi), Fi ve Intermediary 
Pharmacovigilance Centres (National Institutes of ASU & H) and 74 Peripheral 
Pharmacovigilance Centres (35 Ayurveda, 14 Siddha, 11 Unani and 13 Homoeopathy) across 
the country. Technical inputs are being received from Indian Pharmacopoeial Commission; 
CDSCO and WHO-Country Office, New Delhi. 
3.56 Since August 2018, the established network  has taken up the task of surveillance of 
misleading advertisements of ASU & H drugs / systems appearing in print and TV media for 
reporting to State regulatory authorities. Since January 2019, reporting of suspected adverse drug 
reactions has been initiated. More than 10,671 misleading advertisements and 608 Suspected 
Adverse Drug Reactions of ASU & H Drugs have been identified from January, 2019 to 
December, 2020.  COVID-19 related Misleading Advertisements have also been considered 
while reporting and 171 such reports were reported to the respective State Licensing Authorities 
by the Coordinators of Peripheral Pharmacovigilance Centres from April to December, 2020.

bringing legislation for regulation of Yoga and Natur opathy is under active consideration by the

registered Naturopathy practitioners as on 1.1.2018 as per Ministry of AYUSH'S Report

Practitioners. The Committee, therefore, was of the view that bringing a new Bill for 
regulating Yoga and Naturopathy where practitioners are yet to be identified was

Naturopathy in the NCISM Bill instead. However, the NCISM Bill was passed and Yoga

STUDIES AND RESEARCH WORK W.R.T COVID 19 
 
4.6 The Ministry of AYUSH did extensive studies and undertook both curative and 
prophylactic research work through its five research councils and twelve educ ational institutes to 
mitigate the Covid-19 pandemic. The COVID-19 pandemic has provided another opportunity for 
the designing of clinical and field trials adapted to the traditional health systems. The 
prophylactic research work included lifestyle advocac ies to boost immunity which helps the 
prevention of various kinds of infectious diseases. Prophylaxis initiatives included 
Ashwagandha, Chyawanprash, Ayush Kwatha, Guduchi in Ayurveda and Arsenic album 30c in 
Homeopathy. Another important and popular prophylaxis intervention is Yoga, it solves the 
issues of burnout, insomnia and heart rate variability among frontline healthcare workers, 
COVID-19 patients and people in general. Similarly, interventions studies for management of 
COVID-19   included AYUSH –64, Guduchi - Pipali, Ashwagandha –Shunthi, Guduchi in

COVID-19 in Homeopathy.  
 
4.7 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives taken by the Ministry of AYUSH 
through its various institutes in mainstreaming AYUSH systems of medicine. However, the 
Committee is of the opinion that the majority of the work done is preventive in nature and 
recommends that the Ministry should encourage and create a detailed roadmap for 
establishing AYUSH systems of medicine as a curative alternative to the Allopathic system. 
The Committee believes that the Ministry should do more than organizing seminars, 
conferences, meetings, workshops, road shows etc to bring some tangible progress in the 
adoption of Indian traditional systems. The Committee notes the main reason behind the 
poor export of Indian traditional drugs is their failure to meet global norms on safety and 
efficacy. The Committee also notes that licensing of Ayurvedic drugs is a State subjec t, so 
there is a lack of uniformity in the approach of different States.

MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENTS DURING PANDEMIC COVID 19 
 
4.10 The Committee notes that during the Covid-19 period, the Ministry of AYUSH registered 
a sharp spike in complaints against manufacturers of Ayurveda and other traditional products for 
misleading consumers. The Committee has been given to understand that the Ministry received 
over 570 complaints between March and December 2020, related to false, ambiguous and 
misleading claims by manufacturers of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani products. The figure is 
twice the 268 complaints that the ministry registered in March 2019-20. 
 
4.11 The Committee believes that misleading and unfounded advertisements particularly 
by ASU drug makers will force people to gradually d esist from consuming such ASU 
formulations. The Committee recommends that provisions of both the Drugs & Cosm etics 
Act Rules & Magical Remedies Act should be made more stringent to tackle the problem of 
misleading and unfounded advertisements. The Committee desires the Ministry to revisit 
both the period of imprisonment and the fine amount under these rules to re gulate and 
control the violation of the provisions of the said Acts. The licensing authorities and drug 
controllers at the State level must also take prompt actions against any such misconduct.  
 
4.12 The Committee has been given to understand that the Ministry of AYUSH established a 
three-tier network of Pharmacovigilance centres - 01-National; 05-Intermediary and  Peripheral 
Pharmacovigilance Centers. This network has the task of surveillance of misleading 
advertisements of ASU &H drugs/systems in print and  TV media for reporting to State 
regulatory authorities.  
 
4.13 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must ensure stringent 
implementation of Pharmacovigilance schemes. For this, the Committee recommends that 
the education-related to Pharmacovigilance should be included in the curriculum itself and 
periodic awareness programmes should be organized for both health care professionals 
and patients. Moreover, monthly reporting of ADRs (Adverse Drug Reactions) reports 
should be made mandatory at all AYUSH wellness centres. The Committee believes that 
maintaining a comprehensive and updated medicine literature database would provide 
credible and latest medical information to health care professionals. Better sync between 
drug regulators would ensure that authorities are well educated on safety issues in 
everyday practice and thus would be relevant to future regulatory action. The Committee 
desires that the submission of Periodic Safety Update Reports (PSUR) must be made 
mandatory for AYUSH drugs.  The Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate that all 
these measu res can only be realized if the Pharmacovigilance network is provided with 
adequate funds and manpower. The Committee, therefore, strongly desires that the 

46 
 
Ministry should seek adequate funds from the Ministry of Finance (MoF) to strengthen the 
pharmacovigilance network both at the central and regional level.

(Para 3.33) 
 The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry through its medicinal plants 
components under NAM encourages farmers to cultivate medicinal plants by giving 
subsidy for 140 growing prioritized plants. The Committee is, however, constrained to 
observe that this scheme has not been able to make its presence felt throughout the length 
and breadth of the country as a result of which a majority of farmers are not benefited by 

59 
 
it.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this scheme needs to be widely publiciz ed 
and popularized through State Implementing Agencies so that more and more farmers 
from all the States are encouraged to grow medicinal plants and herbs besides routine 
crop. The State Implementing Agencies should also further market linkages so that the  
farmers do not face the problem of finding buyers for their produce. The Committee 
further recommends the SMPBs to encourage the development of clusters of cultivation of 
medicinal plants.  
(Para 3.38) 
 The Committee appreciates that two projects of multi -tier cropping are being done 
in Andhra Pradesh and Haryana.  The Committee recommends the NMPB to expand these 
projects in other States too and also assess the pros and cons of inter -cropping and mono -
plantation.  The Committee desires that NMPB should ex amine the different type of 
cropping for cultivation of medicinal plants should not in any way adversely affect the 
efficacy of the medicinal plants. The Committee, therefore, recommends that research in 
this area of different types of cropping and its eff ect on medicinal plants should be 
conducted so that its outcomes can help in increasing the cultivation of medicinal plants. 
The Ministry should also conduct a research to assess the efficacy of medicinal plants/herbs 
which are not grown in their natural e nvironment. Such a study would help the Ministry 
improve the quality of Ayurveda drugs.  
(Para 3.41) 
 The Committee is anguished to note that the proposal for creation of 24 posts is yet 
not approved.  The Committee, time and again, has been laying emphasi s on having 
adequate manpower for the Board so that it could effectively implement the mandate 
assigned to it.  This laid back approach of the Ministry is not in sync with its objective 
mission of giving impetus to the cultivation, conservation and documen tation of medicinal 
plants. The Committee is of the view that in the absence of adequate manpower the dream 
of achieving the objective cannot be realized  and it, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
accord priority to the human resource requirement of th e Board as it is the nodal agency 
for medicinal plants in the country.  
(Para 3.43) 
 The Committee is deeply disappointed with the status of manpower in the 36 
SMPBs.  Apart from Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, there is no separate regular 
post sanctioned by respective State Government for SMPBs.  The shortage of manpower in 
SMPBs is a matter of serious concern as the NMPB, being the nodal agency for medicinal 
plants cannot function alone without the active support of SMPBs. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Ministry that issue of shortage of manpower in SMPBs 
should be taken up with the States/UTs and they may be convinced of the importance of 
having separate manpower for SMPBs. The Ministry should also have guidelines wherein 
minimum number of manpower required in a SMPB be laid down clearly so that the 
SMPB understand the need to give the support to the NMPB as well as involve itself fully in 
the promotion of the medicinal plants of that State. The Committee strongly believes that 
the schemes of medicinal plant can not be implemented properly till a robust structure in 
the States (SMPBs) with adequate funds and full time manpower is made available.  The 

60 
 
Committee, therefore, exhorts the Ministry to persuade the States/UTs to have separate full 
time manpower for SMPBs for better operational efficacy.  
(Para 3.45) 
QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
 
 The Committee has been emphatically pursuing the issue of quality control and 
scientific validation of AYUSH drugs.  The Committee, however, expresses concerns over 
the reported presence of metals in AYUSH drug formulations and safety of these 
medicines.  Instances of side -effects of AYUSH medicines and other products have also 
come to light.  The Committee believes that a solid and robust quality control mechanism is 
the only way to ensure credibility and safety of AYUSH drugs. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that in order to have scientific validation, more and more clinical 
trials need to be done to fill up the gap due to lack of evidence based medicines.  Given the 
growing popularity of AYUSH systems, it is the need of the hour to lay utmost focus  on 
scientific validation and strong documentation.  The role of Central Drug Controller 
becomes very important in approval of drugs which have undergone pre -clinical trials, 
clinical trials etc.  The Committee, further, believes that publication of peer -reviewed 
papers in reputed international journals will go a long way in establishing the credibility 
and authenticity of AYUSH systems of medicine.  The Committee is also of the view that 
there should be separate and adequate funding for clinical trials and  scientific research 
which should stand international scrutiny so that AYUSH drug get the global recognition 
and acceptability.  
 (Para 3.49) 
 
CENTRAL DRUG CONTROLLER FOR AYUSH DRUGS 
 The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the pace of work be ing done 
for creation/development of a vertical structure in CDSCO.  The low allocation of funds 
and reduction at RE stage in 2020 -21 indicate that the scheme has not taken off as yet.  
There has been inordinate delay in the creation and development of thi s vertical structure 
in CDSCO.  Even the activities mentioned quarter –wise for the year 2021 -22 indicate that 
the Regulatory officials will start work in the last quarter only after Recruitment Rules are 
notified and process of recruitment initiated.  Emp hasizing the need of this structure for 
carrying out the regulatory work in accordance with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, 
the Committee feels that it is high time that this structure is functional with all requisite 
features in place to carry out the s et mandate and ensure good manufacturing practices in 
the AYUSH industry. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that creation of the 
vertical structure should not be delayed any further and all out efforts must be made to 
make CDSCO fully functiona l in the year 2021 -22 so that the envisaged role of this 
structure is carried out with proper fund allocation and utilization.   
(Para 3.52) 
 The Committee observes that even though the E-Aushadhi portal has been launched 
more than two years ago, the numb er of online registration and license application is not 
very encouraging. The Committee believes that the Ministry needs to engage the 
States/UTs and incentivize them to encourage the manufacturers, drug inspectors to use 

61 
 
the portal so as to increase tran sparency, improve data accessibility of  AYUSH medicines 
and provide real -time information of the licensed manufacturers; which are the key 
features of the portal. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should come out with 
clear guidelines stating tha t AYUSH manufactures should have in -house drug testing 
laboratories duly approved by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and 
Calibration Laboratories and also to ensure stringent practicing of WHO prescribed Good 
Manufacturing Practices (GMP). 
(Para 3.54) 
PHARMACOVIGILANCE INITIATIVES FOR ASU&H DRUGS 
 The Committee is in full agreement with the findings of the Comprehensive Impact 
Assessment  of the scheme wherein it has been noted that due to insufficient manpower, it 
would be difficult to achieve the objectives of the scheme and therefore the scheme needs 
to be strengthened with skilled manpower.  The Committee is of the firm view that even 
though the network of the Pharmacovigilance centres has increased in the States/UTs, the 
scheme is not being implemented properly due to shortage of manpower.  The Committee 
is also of the view that the meager allocation for Pharmacovigilance Initiative would  
certainly not help in achieving the desired objectives. The Committee wonders that the 
projected requirement for the scheme was just Rs. 2.83 crore in 2020-21 and the allocation 
was Rs. 2.80 crore in BE 2020 -21.  It seems to the Committee that the Ministr y is not 
planning to enhance the reach of the scheme given the demand for funds for this scheme.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to make available adequate 
resources, including manpower for Pharmacovigilance centres across the country  and 
visualize the potential of the scheme and accordingly project its demand for substantial 
funds for effective implementation of the scheme.  
(Para 3.64) 
RESEARCH COUNCILS 
 The Committee notes with concern that as compared to 2019 -20, the utilization 
trend in 2020 -21 has been poor. The Committee, therefore, recommends that each 
Research Council must draw a fiscal roadmap and make every attempt to fully utilize the 
allocated funds.   
(Para 3.69) 
 The Committee has been given to understand that a ll the Res earch Councils under 
AYUSH are fully funded by the Government of India. The Committee also notes the 
various initiatives carried out by CCRAS for generating revenue from external sources.  
The Committee, however, notes that there has been a decrease in the  earning of the 
CCRAS over the last two years.  The Committee would expect that each Research Council 
to make constant and concerted efforts to enhance its internal resource generation capacity 
so as to match the Government funding.  
(Para 3.71) 
 
 

62 
 
NABH ACCREDITATION 
 The Committee is of the view that obtaining NABH accreditation is essential to gain 
the confidence of the people and to remain competitive in the field of health services. 
Further accreditation would ensure improvement in the quality and competency of the 
Institute as well. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to ensure 
that all the AYUSH institutes must expedite the process for NABH accreditation and 
ensure its compliance with the NABH standards. The Institutes must endeavour towards 
improving their capacity and implementing NABH standards in their organization. The 
Committee also recommends all the Institutes under the Research Councils to shed off the 
lackadaisical attitude and set a timeframe for completing the NABH Accreditation pr ocess 
so that unwarranted delays are avoided.  
(Para 3.76) 
QUALITY ASSURANCE OF DRUGS AVAILABLE IN THE MARKET 
 The Committee, while taking note of the submission of the Ministry, observes that 
ensuring Quality assurance of  AYUSH drugs comes under the juris diction of State Drugs 
Controllers, is apprehensive about the required technical expertise and the presence of a 
separate Department exclusively for testing AYUSH drugs in States Drugs 
Controlling/Licensing Authorities. The Committee, therefore, feels that  AYUSH is in 
urgent need of a more robust drug quality assurance system that is AYUSH centric. A 
separate independent regulating body at the State level which focuses on ensuring that only 
the best quality AYUSH drugs are available in the market will go a long way in 
mainstreaming AYUSH healthcare services in the country. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends for creation of a specialized body specifically for AYUSH Drug Control which 
has the required technical staff with requisite expertise in AYUSH at the State level on 
lines of the vertical structure for AYUSH under CDSCO.  
(Para 3.82) 
 The Committee also notes that CCRUM has its own Drug Testing Laboratories and 
Drug Standardization Research Centers for assurance of quality drugs. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to make constant efforts for increasing the number of such Labs 
in the country.  
(Para 3.83) 
NEW DRUGS  
 The Committee takes note of the initiatives carried out by the Councils for the 
formulation of new drugs. The Committee, however, recommends the Councils to carry out 
well designed clinical trials. The Councils must also collaborate with other Institutes and 
publish research papers in high end journals for better scientific validation of AYUSH 
drugs.  
(Para 3.89) 
 The Committee recommends t he Ministry of AYUSH to prepare a list of medicines 
of its own system meant for common man's knowledge to be readily available for used in 

63 
 
case of minor -illness like routine fatigue, headache and stomachache, etc. The Committee, 
however, does not approve self -medicine.  
(Para 3.90) 
PROPOSED LEGISLATION FOR PROMOTION AND REGULATION OF YOGA AND 
NATUROPATHY 
 The Committee, in its 115th Report on NCISM Bill, had observed that the number of 
registered Naturopathy practitioners as on 1.1.2018 as per Ministry of AYUSH'S Report 
"Ayush in India" was 2485. The 115 th Report on NCISM Bill made no mention of Yoga 
Practitioners. The Committee, therefore, was of the view that bringing a new Bill for 
regulating Yoga and Naturopathy where practitioners are yet to be identif ied was 
unwarranted. The Committee had therefore recommended for inclusion of Yoga and 
Naturopathy in the NCISM Bill instead. However, the NCISM Bill was passed and Yoga 
and Naturopathy was not included in the Bill.  The Committee accordingly, feels that t here 
is an urgent need to create an overarching body for regulation of Yoga and Naturopathy in 
the country. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to expedite the 
formulation of legislation for regulation of Yoga and Naturopathy. 
(Para 3.92) 
 The Committee visualizes the immense potential in AYUSH for its advancement as a 
lifestyle choice. The Committee has time and again highlighted the benefits of Yoga and 
advocated its inclusion in School curriculum. The Committee therefore, reiterate s its 
recommendation to include Yoga and specific modules on AYUSH in the School 
curriculum.   The Committee is of the considered view that Yoga and Naturopathy contain 
potential for not only employment generation capacity but would also promote the 'Fit 
India Programme'.  
(Para 3.93) 
AYUSH RESPONSE IN COVID 19 PANDEMIC 
 The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s efforts to get feedback from the citizens 
on its initiatives and measures and impact on the prevention of COVID -19 by using the 
AYUSH drugs. The Committee is heartened to note that the 89.8% of the total respondents 
have benefitted from the practice of AYUSH advisory and measures for the prevention of 
COVID-19. The Committee also commends the AYUSH doctors for stepping up and 
playing a significant rol e in mitigating the Covid pandemic. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry must put in place strict guidelines to check false generation 
of data by the state level AYUSH boards to achieve the allotted targets.  
(Para 4.5) 
STUDIES AND RESEARCH WORK W.R.T COVID 19 
 
 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives taken by the Ministry of AYUSH 
through its various institutes in mainstreaming AYUSH systems of medicine. However, the 
Committee is of the opinion that the majority of the work done is preven tive in nature and 
recommends that the Ministry should encourage and create a detailed roadmap for 

64 
 
establishing AYUSH systems of medicine as a curative alternative to the Allopathic system. 
The Committee believes that the Ministry should do more than organ izing seminars, 
conferences, meetings, workshops, road shows etc to bring some tangible progress in the 
adoption of Indian traditional systems. The Committee notes the main reason behind the 
poor export of Indian traditional drugs is their failure to meet global norms on safety and 
efficacy. The Committee also notes that licensing of Ayurvedic drugs is a State subject, so 
there is a lack of uniformity in the approach of different States. 
(Para 4.7) 
COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH/CLINICAL TRIALS ON MITIGATION OF COVID-19 
WITH INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS 
 
 The Committee appreciates the research work done by the Ministry of AYUSH 
through its research institutions in collaboration with foreign institutes. The Committee is 
of the opinion that the joint research work would increase the acceptability of the AYUSH  
systems in the International arena. The joint research work also helps in allaying concerns 
regarding rejection of AYUSH drugs by foreign drug regulators due to the presence of 
constituent components beyond the permissible limits. The Committee recommends  that 
the Ministry should actively work towards creating demand for Indian Traditional drugs 
in foreign countries. Once the local population starts demanding such drugs, the stringent 
safety norms which are not considerate of the nuances of the traditional  medicines system 
would be relaxed by the respective countries. The Ministry should also work towards 
establishing an India led global alliance for traditional drugs to facilitate better knowledge 
sharing, collaborative research, exchange of ideas & best p ractices and formulate common 
standards for quality control. A global alliance with a headquarters preferably in India 
would not only give a sense of legitimacy to the AYUSH systems but also help in 
mainstreaming it.   
(Para 4.9) 
MISLEADING ADVERTISEMENTS DURING PANDEMIC COVID 19 
 
 The Committee believes that misleading and unfounded advertisements particularly 
by ASU drug makers will force people to gradually d esist from consuming such ASU 
formulations. The Committee recommends that provisions of both the Drugs & Cosmetics 
Act Rules & Magical Remedies Act should be made more stringent to tackle the problem of 
misleading and unfounded advertisements. The Committee desires the Ministry to revisit 
both the period of imprisonment and the fine amount under these  rules to regulate and 
control the violation of the provisions of the said Acts. The licensing authorities and drug 
controllers at the State level must also take prompt actions against any such misconduct.  
 
(Para 4.11) 
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must ensure stringent 
implementation of Pharmacovigilance schemes. For this, the Committee recommends that 
the education-related to Pharmacovigilance should be included in the curriculum itself and 
periodic awareness programmes should be organized for both health care professionals 
and patients. Moreover, monthly reporting of ADRs (Adverse Drug Reactions) reports 
should be made mandatory at all AYUSH wellness centres. The Committee believes that 
maintaining a comprehensive and updated medicine literature database would provide 

65 
 
credible and latest medical information to health care professionals. Better sync between 
drug regulators would ensure that authorities are well educated on safety issues in 
everyday practice and thus would be relevant to future regulatory action. The Committee 
desires that the submission of Periodic Safety Update Reports (PSUR) must be made 
mandatory for AYUSH drugs.  The Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate that all 
these measu res can only be realized if the Pharmacovigilance network is provided with 
adequate funds and manpower. The Committee, therefore, strongly desires that the 
Ministry should seek adequate funds from the Ministry of Finance (MoF) to strengthen the 
pharmacovigilance network both at the central and regional level.  
(Para 4.13) 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT: Vacant posts in Research Councils and 
Educational Institutes of AYUSH 
 
 The Committee is constrained to note large number of vacant positions in AYUSH 
Research Councils and other Institutions.  The Committee feels that manpower is the key 
to success of any institution and the lofty objectives of each of the Councils/Institutes  would 
remain only on paper without the people in position.  The Committee understands that 
pandemic Covid-19 may have delayed the recruitment process last year but it is high time 
that the process is expedited and completed in the year but it is high time that the process is 
expedited and completed in the year 2021 -22.  The Committee strongly recommends to the 
Ministry to prioritize this area of concern and take swift measures to fill up the vacant 
posts.   
(Para 4.22) 
POSHAN ABHIYAN 
 The Committee is given to understand that the Ministry of AYUSH in collaboration 
with the Ministry of WCD will run a pilot programme in AWCs for testing the efficacy of 
nutritional support for addressing mal -nutrition and mal -nourishment. The Committee 
appreciates the initiati ves of the Ministry for addressing under -nutrition, stunting in 
children and anaemia in women. The Committee would like the Ministry to expedite its 
initiatives in the 3000 AWCs which would go a long way in addressing the problem of mal -
nutrition. 
(Para 4.24) 
MEDICAL TOURISM IN AYUSH 
 
 The Committee appreciates the pivotal role of AYUSH systems of medicine during 
the pandemic Covid -19 when the AYUSH systems occupied the mental space of common 
masses who got the benefits of boosting the immune system agai nst the pandemic at time of 
dire need of saving lives. Owing to the largely believed notion of negligible side -effects 
associated with the AYUSH drugs and measures, AYUSH systems particularly, Yoga, 
Ayurveda and Homeopathy became very popular among people both locally and globally. 
To build on this newfound popularity, the Committee recommends that the Ministry must 
take concerted efforts like setting up a dedicated AYUSH promotion desk in Indian 

66 
 
embassies to make the AYUSH system a viable alternative abroa d. The Committee should 
project AYUSH systems as a means for the holistic well being of an individual acting as 
platform to achieve the objectives of Budget 2021 -22. The Committee also recommends 
that the Ministry should facilitate students’ exchange progr ammes as such initiatives will 
broaden the perspectives and understandings of the students. Also, foreign students coming 
to India and understanding AYUSH systems from close quarters will act as brand 
ambassadors of the AYUSH systems in their respective co untries. The Ministry may 
approach celebrities to act as brand ambassadors of AYUSH systems in global arena.  
(Para 4.26) 
OUTPUT-OUTCOME FRAMEWORK FOR SCHEMES 2021-22 
 The Committee has taken into consideration the output -outcome framework for 
schemes of Ministry of AYUSH which envelops financial outlay, targets sets for outputs 
and outcome during 2021-22. The Committee hopes that the financial outlay earmarked for 
various schemes would create the enabling environment and bring forth catalectic change 
in the basic infrastructure for AYUSH education and research and improve the AYUSH 
healthcare services.  The Committee is of the considered view that the budgetary allocatio n 
to the Centre Sector Schemes and National AYUSH Mission would definitely improve the 
quality of AYUSH health care facilities in the country. The Committee hopes that all the 
projects undertaken during 2021 -22 would be completed without time and cost over run 
especially construction projects at National Institutes. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry of AYUSH to strengthen its monitoring mechanism to oversee the execution of 
research projects and to ensure that physical targets set during the year are ach ieved. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to undertake annual performance evaluation of 
each scheme and programme through cost benefit analysis and SWOT analysis. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry should formulate output -outcome framework for  
remaining years of 15th Finance Commission in order to have a holistic overview of the 
schemes under the Ministry. The Committee, while taking into account the financial and 
the physical achievement under various schemes of the Ministry, recommends the following 
organizational interventions for improvements:-  
(i) Advance planning to be made for completion of various formalities so that the 
process of sanctioning and release of funds for the various projects be started 
in the beginning of the next financial year. 
(ii) More workshops and review meetings to be organized for addressing the issues 
in the implementation of the schemes.  
(iii) More field visits to be organized for onsite appraisal of progress of 
implementation of the schemes 
(iv)  Dashboard for online monitoring of schemes and programmes. 
(Para 4.27) 
 
 

67 
 
PROGRESSIVE LEGISLATION AND INTEGRATED HEALTH MANAGEMENT 
 The Committee believes that all progressive legislation undertaken by the 
Government aims at focusing integrated Health and Well -being and that is the guiding 
philosophy of the Budget 2021 -22. The Committee has already supported the adoption of 
an inclusive and integrated health care policy. The Committee believes that AYUSH and its 
holistic approach to promoting preventive and holistic healt hcare must also be 
strengthened. The Committee, in this regard, again impresses upon the Government to 
expedite the process of piloting the Yoga and the Naturopathy Bill, to give further impetus 
to the integrated and holistic approach to the Health and Well-being.  
(Para 4.29) 
 The Committee observes that the trend of diseases as well as severity of illnesses has 
undergone a substantial change in the modern age. Advancement in modern science has 
brought out a revolution in the way one identifies, diagnoses and treats illnesses now -a-
days. The Committee believes that AYUSH with its traditional/classic knowledge has 
immense potential in devising a holistic approach against the ever changing challenges in 
the health sector and ensuring good health of the masses . However, AYUSH has remained 
neglected and modern system of medicine, with a scientific evidence base, has 
overshadowed AYUSH's popularity and growth. Nevertheless, the Committee observes 
that with the formation of a separate Ministry for AYUSH, various e fforts have been made 
for the revival of AYUSH over the years. The Committee appreciates the Schemes and 
Programmes implemented by the Ministry of AYUSH for mainstreaming of AYUSH 
services and acknowledges its satisfactory trend of budgetary utilization. T he Committee 
also believes that it is high time to make AYUSH more competitive and expand its outreach 
across States as well as in the international market. The Committee believes that for 
strengthening AYUSH research, education institutes, its industry an d the quality of 
AYUSH healthcare, a substantial enhancement in budgetary allocation is the need of the 
hour. AYUSH must also collaborate and coordinate with other scientific disciplines as well 
as the modern system of medicine.  Integration of AYUSH with modern advances will 
enhance its reliability and scientifically validate the ancient AYUSH traditions.  
(Para 4.30)

CHAPTER - I 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
 MISSION STATEMENT OF THE BILL 
 
 1.1 The Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Bill,  2020 provides  for the 
regulation and s upervision of the assisted reproductive technology clinics and the assisted 
reproductive technology banks, prevention of misuse, safe and ethical practice of assisted 
reproductive technology services and for matters connected therewith or incidental theret o. 
The Bill intends to protect the affected women and children from exploitation , support the 
oocyte donor with an insurance cover, regulate multiple embryo implantation and protect the 
children born through ART. The Bill, further, aims to regulate cryopreservation of sperm, 
oocytes and embryo by the ART Banks  and intends to make Pre-Genetic Implantation 
Testing mandatory for  pre-existing, heritable or genetic diseases only  for the benefit of the 
child born through assisted reproductive technology. 
 
 NECESSITY OF THE BILL 
 
 1.2 According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons (SOR) of the Bill, t he Assisted 
Reproductive Technology (ART)  has grown  rapidly in the last few years and India has 
registered the highest growth  in the ART centres and the number of A RT cycles performed 
every year. Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART), including In Vitro Fertilization 
(IVF), has given hope to a many persons suffering from infertility but introduced a plethora 
of legal, ethical and social issues.  
 
1.2.1 As per t he background note on the Bill furnished by the Ministry , India has become 
one of the major centres of this global fertility industry  over the years , with reproductive 
medical tourism becoming a significant activity. Clinics in India offer nearly all the ART 
services—gamete donation, intrauterine insemination (IUI), In-vitro fertilization ( IVF), 
Intracytoplasmic sperm injection ( ICSI), Pre-implantation Genetic Testing (PGT)  and 
gestational surrogacy.  The reproductive segment of the Indian medical tourism market is 
valued at more than $450 million a year and was forecast by the ICMR to be a six billion 
dollar a year market in 2008. India ’s fertility industry in  is an integral part of the country's 
growing medical tourism industry, which experienced 30% growth in 2 000 and 15% growth 
between 2005 and 2010. Despite so much activity in India, there is no standardisation of 
protocols yet and reporting is still very inadequate. Furthermore, there are only guidelines of 
ART, and no law still exists. There has been debate on the medical, ethical and legal aspects 
of ARTs. 
 
OBJECTIVES OF THE BILL 
 
1.3  The ART Bill seeks to provide the following: 
 
(i) To regulate the ART services and protect the affected women and children from 
exploitation. 

2 
 
(ii) To support the oocyte donor by an insurance cover and protection from multiple 
embryo implantation. 
(iii) To provide rights to children born through assisted reproductive technology 
equivalent to rights provided to biological children.  
(iv) To regulate cryopreservation of sperms, oocytes and embryos by the ART 
banks. 
(v) To make Pre-Implantation Genetic Testing mandatory for the benefit of the 
child born through assisted reproductive technology. 
(vi) To ensure proper registration of ART clinics and banks. 
 
ORIGIN OF THE BILL 
 
1.4 The world's first test tu be baby, Louise Brown was born o n 25th July 1978. About two 
months later, the world's second and India's first IVF baby, Kanupriya alias Durga was born  
in Ko lkata. Since then the field of Assisted Reproductive T echnology (ART) has grown 
exponentially. India has become one of the major centers of the ART resulting in multitude  
of legal, ethical and social issues  and there were no standardizing protocols available. The 
ICMR drafted the National Guidelines for Accreditation, Supervision and Regulation of 
ART Clinics in India in 2005 as the first ever national guidelines for laying down standards 
of conduct for surrogacy in India. The Law Commission  of India  suo motu took up the 
subject of the need for legislation to regulate Assisted Reproductive Technology Clinics as  
well as rights and obligations of parties to a surrogacy. Th e Commission presented its 228 th 
Report in 2009 which  stated that an a ctive legislative intervention is required to facilitate 
correct uses of the new technology, i.e. ART and legalization of surrogacy.  
 
1.4.1 The Departmental-Related Standing Committee on  Health and Family Welfare, in its 
One Hundred Second Report on Surrogacy Regulation Bill, 2016 had observed as follows: 
 
"The Committee strongly believes that with the rapid advancement of scie nce 
and technology in all spheres of life, there is an urgent need to regulate the use 
of modern techniques especially w.r.t. assisted reproduction and use of ART for 
surrogacy. Hence, the Committee feels that along with surrogacy regulation, 
there is urge nt need to regulate the ART clinics across the country. It is a fact 
that surrogacy procedures cannot be conducted without assisted reproduction 
techniques and therefore, mere enactment of the Surrogacy Bill would not serve 
the purpose of controlling comme rcialization of the surrogacy facilities across 
the country in the absence of regulation of assisted reproductive clinics and 
banks where surrogacy is being conducted as ART Clinics and Surrogacy 
Clinics are not separate. The Committee, therefore, strongly  recommends that 
the ART Bill should be brought forth before the Surrogacy (Regulation), Bill, 
2016." 
 
1.4.2 Furthermore, the Select Committee on the Surrogacy ( Regulation) Bill, 2019, has 
recommended that ART Bill should be brought before the Surrogacy (R egulation) Bill, 
2019, so that all the highly technical and medical aspects could be addressed adequately in 
the Surrogacy (Regulation) Bill, 201 9.  It also  recommended that the National and State 

3 
 
Boards constituted for the regulation of surrogacy as propo sed in the Bill shall act as t he 
Boards for regulation of ART. 
  
 1.4.3 Consequently, the ART (Regulation) Bill, 2020 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 
September 14, 2020  and was  referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Health an d Family Welfare, Rajya Sabha  by Chairman, Rajya Sabha in 
consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha on October 3 rd, 2020 for examination and Report. 
On further recommendation of the Committee, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha has 
extended the time of submission of Report by 1st April, 2021. 
 
 THE SALIENT FEATURES OF THE BILL  
 
1.5  As per information provided by the Department of Health Research, the salient features 
of the Bill are as follows: 
 
1) “assisted reproductive technology”  means all techniques that a ttempt 
to obtain a pregnancy by handling the sperm or the oocyte outside the 
human body and transferring the gamete or the embryo into the 
reproductive tract of a woman;  
2) “assisted reproductive technology clinic”  means any premises 
equipped with requisite facilities and medical practitioners registered 
with the National Medical Commission of India for carrying out the 
procedures related to the assisted reproductive technology; 
3) “commissioning couple”  means an infertile Married couple who 
approaches an assist ed reproductive technology clinic or assisted 
reproductive technology bank for obtaining  services that the assisted 
reproductive technology clinic or the assisted reproductive technology 
bank is authorized to provide; 
4) “Woman” means any woman above the leg al age of marriage who 
approach an assisted reproductive technology clinic or assisted 
reproductive technology bank for obtaining  services that the assisted 
reproductive technology clinic or the assisted reproductive technology 
bank is authorized to provide; 
5) The National Board shall be the same Board a s proposed in the  
Surrogacy Bill with 24 members,  which will be c haired by Minister in 
Charge of Health and Family Welfare.  
6) The State Board shall be the same Board as proposed in the Surrogacy 
Bill with 21 Members. The Board will be c haired by Minister-in-charge 
of Health and Family Welfare in the State.  
7) The existing assisted reproductive technology clinics and  the assisted 
reproductive technology banks, as on the date of the enactment of the 
Act, conductin g Assisted reproductive technology procedures partly or 
exclusively shall make an application to the  State authority and after 
registration submit the same to the  National Registry within such period 
and in such form, manner and  with such fee as may be prescribed within 
a period of sixty days from the date of appointment. 

4 
 
8) The assisted reproductive technology services shall be available to a 
woman above the legal age of marriage and below the age of fifty years. 
9)  The assisted reproductive technology servi ces shall be available to a 
man above the legal age of marriage and below the age of fifty five 
years. 
10) An oocyte donor shall be an ever married woman having at least one live 
child of her own with a minimum age of three years and shall donate 
oocytes only once in her life and not more than seven oocyte shall be 
retrieved from the oocyte donor. 
11) The assisted reproductive  technology clinics shall provide professional 
counselling to commissioning couple about all the implications and 
chances of success of assisted reproductive technology procedures in the 
clinic and shall also inform the commissioning couple of the advantages, 
disadvantages and cost of the procedures, their medical side effects, 
risks including the risk of multiple pregnancy, the possibility of 
adoption, and any such other matter as may help the couple arrive at a n 
informed decision that would most likely be the best for the couple. 
12) The assisted reproductive technology clinics and assisted reproductive 
technology banks shall ensure that commissio ning couple and donors of 
gametes are eligible to avail of assisted reproductive technology 
procedures.  
13) The child born through Assisted reproductive technology shall be 
deemed to be a biological child of the commissioning couple and the 
said child shall b e entitled to all the rights and privileges available to a 
natural child only from the commissioning couple under any law for the 
time being in force. 
14) Sex selection shall not be permitted as per clause- 26. 
15) The Pre -implantation Genetic testing shall be use d only to screen the 
human embryo for known, pre -existing, heritable or genetic diseases or 
for such other purposes as may be prescribed. 
16) Contraventions to the provisions of the Act for sex selection shall be 
punishable with a term which shall not be less than five years but may 
extend to ten years or with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh 
rupees but may extend to twenty-five lakh rupees or with both. 
17) Abandoning or exploit ing the child/c hildren, selling embryo/gam ete, 
exploiting commissioning woman and couple, shall invite a penalty with 
imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than eight years but may 
extend to twelve years and with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh 
rupees but may extend to twenty lakh rupees. 
 
1.6 As per the backgr ound note received from the Department of Health Research, the 
proposed Bill seeks to have the following legislative impact: 
 
1) Registration of all ART clinics and Banks 
2) Control of unethical Assisted Reproductive Technology practices 
including gamete donation;   

5 
 
3) Improve the quality of Assisted Reproductive Technology services;  
4) Decrease the cost of Assisted Reproduction treatment; 
5) Conduct research on new emerging areas of Assisted Reproduction and 
develop low cost Assisted Reproductive Technology for the economically 
weaker section of the society; 
6) Develop polic ies and guidelines from time to time on Assisted 
Reproduction; 
7) Infertile couples will be more sure of the ethical practices in ART clinics 
and Banks; 
8) Medical Tourism will have more assurances of ethical practice in India. 
 
1.6.1   Summarizing the overall legislative impact of the ART Bill, the representative of 
DHR stated as under: 
 
“ The impact would be that it would bring about the registration of all the clinics, 
it would control unethical ART practice s, it would improve the quality of ART 
services, it would facilitate framing of requisite policies as we would be having all 
the data and, most importantly, the needy couples would be more sure of the 
ethical practice of ART.” 
 
INTERNATIONAL SCENARIO 
 
1.7  As per information provided by the Ministry of External Affairs,  there are no 
international conventions or treaties in force to deal with ART and States are regulating ART 
at domestic level.  For instance, in June 2020, Australia adopted the Assisted Rep roductive 
Treatment Amendment Act 2020  to amend the Assisted Reproductive Treatment Act 2008, 
to remove the requirement for police checks and child protection order checks before a 
woman (and if applicable, her partner) can start assisted reproductive treatments. 
 
 1.7.1 In May 2020, Ireland amended the Child and  Family Relationship Act 2015. These 
amendments relate to ART and include, among other matters, the possibility for same -sex 
female partners to establish legal parentage from birth and the prohibiti on of anonymous 
gamete donation. 
 
 1.7.2 The state of New York, USA, in April 2020 passed the Child -Parent Security Act 
(CPSA).  The CPSA aims to regulate the establishment of legal parentage, in particular in the 
context o f children conceived through ART .  In state of Rhode Island, USA, the Uniform 
Parentage Act was scheduled to take effect in January 2021.  It includes regulations of ART 
(including access to information on gamete donors) and (commercial) surrogacy 
arrangements (where it provides that the intending parents are to be recognized as the child’s 
legal parents from birth). 
 
 1.7.3 France, Philippines and Switzerland are also considering Bills/legislations in this area . 
In France, the Parliament is considering a bill that would extend access to fertility treatments, 
including gamete donations, to single women and female same -sex couples.  The bill would 
also put an end to anonymity in gamete donations so tha t children born through ART  can 

6 
 
have access to non-identifying information about their donor(s).  Philippines is considering a 
bill that will remove the distinction between ‘legitimate’ and ‘illegitimate’ children (which 
has consequences on their rights, in particular, to inheritance).  The bill also seeks to add 
clarity for children born as a r esult of ART (including where a third-party donor is involved) 
or as a result of an altruistic surrogacy arrangement by deeming such children as being born 
within the wedlock of the intending parents.  The Parliament of Switzerland is considering a 
bill th at would extend access to fertility treatments to single women and female same -sex 
couples. 
 
 1.7.4 Taking into consideration the international Legislative march towards regulating 
the ART services and the incidental issues, the Committee feels that it is incumbent 
upon Government of India to proceed ahead with the progressive legislation on ART 
services as proposed through the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Bill, 
2020. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

7 
 
CHAPTER - II 
 
VIEWS OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH RESEARCH 
 
 2.1    The Committee started its deliberations on the said Bill by hearing the views of the 
Department of Health Research  on the objectives envisaged and the likely impact  including 
challenges to be faced in the implementation of the various provisions of the Bi ll, necessity 
of having two separate legis lations for  ART and Surrogacy etc. The Department of Health 
Research informed the Committee that in 2015 deliberations were held regarding the 
Surrogacy Bill and Assisted Reproductive Technology Bill  and it  was de cided that these  
Bills should be separate but should be placed for consideration simultaneously. It was 
further informed that at the time of deliberations on the Surrogacy Bill, it was felt that these 
two Bills are related and there sh ould be a common Boar d to have control over it both at 
Central and State level.  
 
 2.1.2 During the course of the presentation before the Committee, the Department of Health 
Research apprised that in one of the studies of trend analysis by ICMR, it is estimated that 
the fertility industry would be a 6 billion USD industry by the year 2030.  It is all the more 
substantiated by the fact that fertility rate has declined from 2.7 children in 2005 -06 to 2.1 
per woman as per the National Health Family Survey.  
 
2.1.3 The ART services include the following services :- 
 
a) Ovarian stimulation,  
b) Egg Retrieval, 
c) Invitro fertilisation-IVF,  
d) Intra-Uterine Insemination-IUI,  
e) Intracytoplasmic sperm injection-ICSI,  
f) Embryo transfer,  
g) Gamete Intrafallopian Transfer-GIFT,  
h) Zygote Intra fallopian transfer-ZIFT,  
i) Microsurgical epididymal sperm aspiration -MESA,  
j) Testicular sperm extraction-TESE,  
k) Percutaneous epididymal sperm aspiration-PESA,  
l) Cryopreservation of gametes and embryo.  
 
2.1.4  The Ministry highlighted that ART procedures could be exploited in the fo llowing 
ways: 
 
a) Negligence in performing surgical procedure of harvesting eggs from a 
woman’s body.  
b) Egg retrieval is done from young unmarried girls in many parts of the country. 
c) Unethical preservation of ovum and sperm in ART banks,  
d) Sex selection in procedures of ART clinics,  
e) Multiple embryo implantation,  
f) ART banks advertising for Caucasian donor gamete,  

8 
 
g) Mixing of sperm samples by banks,
