1.144 The Committee is of the view that since COVID is an unknown virus across the world,  
research is going forward to unravel the mystery of the virus constantly mutating itself. It 
remains to be seen how COVID -19 evolves further and what symptoms do the survivors may 
experience. Further, it has been observed that the virus spreads to many di fferent organs of the 
body like the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, lungs, and brain. The Committee believes that there is 
a need for multidisciplinary care service involving several specialists from both the systems i.e., 
Allopathy and AYUSH system of medi cine for the evaluation and the follow -up of patients 
suffered with COVID-19 disease.

COVID complications.

1.154 The Committee observes that the limited healthcare infrastructure in the country has 
further been overburdened while coping up with the rising Covid cases in the country. The

should move towards the noble vision of Universal Health coverage. For this to happen, the

Financing the Health Sector 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.180 The Committee reiterates its  considered view that the healthcare spending in India is 
abysmally low for an emerging economy with a population of 1.3 billion. Lack of desired level of 
investment in the health infrastructure has so far resulted into fragility of Indian health 
ecosystem which posed a big hurdle in generating an effective response against the pandemic. 
The Committee has time and again recommended the Ministry for increasing its spending in the 
health sector for ensuring better health infrastructure and health services to the needy common 
masses. The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the Government's reluctance to act 
upon the Committee's recommendations in letter and spirit. The Committee is assured that the 
serious impact of the pandemic could have been min imized had the Government over the years 
increased its investment in the healthcare system. The Committee is pained to note the trauma 
and distress the public had to undergo due to absence of a dedicated healthcare system. The 
Committee, therefore, strongl y recommends the Government to increase its investments in the 
public healthcare system and make consistent efforts to achieve the National Health Policy 
targets of expenditure up to 2.5% of GDP within two years as the set timeframe of year 2025 is 
far away and the public health cannot be jeopardized till that time schedule. 
                             (Para 8.10) 
1.181 The Committee is of the view that pandemic Covid -19 offers a window to revisit the 
country‟s health policy with the purpose of strengthening the health sector, and thus necessitates 
a higher investment in creating permanent basic health infrastructure. The Committee also 
believes that a higher budgetary allocation will also boost the healthcare industry and shift the 
focus to Indi an manufacturers and domestic supply chain of products. The Committee believes 
that it is the opportune time to boost India‟s healthcare infrastructure and push for greater 
technology deepening in the healthcare sector. 
                             (Para 8.12)

 Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)

2.8 The Committee however differs from the viewpoint of the Ministry as it feels that all the

2.9 The definition of „Mitigation‟, as per Disaster Management Act, 2005, includes measures

whereas a mitigation plan, intends to protect the at-risk population and Vulnerable populations to 
reduce the morbidity and mortality on such populations. Conceptually the two approaches are 
different and hence Ministry of Health & FW continues with its containment plans to 
break/suppress the chain of transmission.

Further Recommendation 
3.5 In view of the loss of life during the second wave of the Covid -19 pandemic, the 
Committee believes that the measures taken by the Ministry to contain/prevent spread of 
SARS-COV-2 proved to be squarely inadequate. The Committee believes that focus should 
be on strengthening of health infrastructure, ensuring adequate availability of beds, 
adequate supply of oxygen cylinders and essential medicines etc . Besides, the G overnment 
must aggressively keep pushing the vaccination program me in terms of granting approval 
to more vaccines, ramping up vaccines’ production, enhancing delivery capacity and 
increasing the vaccination rate.  
 
3.6 With the incidence of highly mutated Omicron (B.1.1.529) strain of Covid virus, the 
Committee strongly believes that the efficacy of the vaccines must be evaluated. The concerns 
with regards to the new strain developing immunoescape mechanism need to be critically 
addressed. The Committee apprehends that rise in mutations in the virus may lead to reporting 
of more virulent and transmissi ble strain of C ovid virus  in the country . The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to adopt Zero Tolerance C ovid-19 Policy and

the exponential growth of COVID cases in the country. The Committee is also worried at the use 

61 
 
of less reliable diagnostic tests which increase the chances of false negatives. Though the Rapid 
Antigen Tests may give faster results but are less reliable than the gold standard RT -PCR tests. 
Large scale use of such tests with low specificity and sensitivity may end up giving false 
negatives and subsequently derail the Covid -19 containment strategy. The Committee is of the 
view that the Government must assess the veracity of Rapid Antigen Test vis -à-vis RT-PCR and 
other diagnostic tests conducted to bring forth the true picture of the testing capacity in the 
country.  
3.8 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to ramp up the testing 
facilities in the country for more accurate tests. The Committee strongly recommends the testing 
rate through the more reliable RT-PCR tests.

Action Taken 
3.9 A joint letter has been issued by Secretary, Health & Family Welfare and Secretary, 
Department of Health Research & DG, ICMR to all States on 9th Dec 2020. Following issues 
have been conveyed to the States: 
o RATs should be used for diagnosis of pre -symptomatic or early symptomatic individuals 
where the viral load is expected to be high.  
o Their use in patients who present after 5 - 7 days of onset of symptoms is not 
recommended.  
o RATs must not take precedence over RT -PCR tests. The use of RATs should be 
restricted to < 30 - 40% in the States.  
o Strictly follow the ICMR algorithm for using RATs to avoid missing of cases.

being procured by them.

testing.

Further Recommendation 
3.11 The Committee bel ieves that timely  detection and isolation of potentially infectious 
people is very crucial in reducing the impact of the pandemic  Covid-19. The importance of 
diagnostic testing therefore, cannot be overlooked. An efficient and widely  deployed testing 
mechanism will go a long way in preventing  the spread of the infection . The Committee is 
pained to note that although the second wave came almost six months after the peak of the 
first wave, India’s testing infrastructure remained abysm al and highly insufficient. The 
Committee is of the opinion that to contain pandemic Covid-19 and its mutated strains, 
India must realise its full testing capacity and augment ’s this capacity even further. The 
government should ensure that the testing should  far o utpace the growth of the cases to 
arrest future waves of Covid-19 early.

work. During the second wave new cases surged as hi gh as 4.5 lakhs a day in April, 2021 
and more than 4 lakh infected persons have died of Covid -19, therefore, inadequate testing 
does not provide the clear picture of the transmission on the ground. The Committee 
recommends t hat the Ministry and authority c oncerned must plan testing a s one -step 
ahead of virus transmission so that infected people are traced and quarantined early, which 
help in breaking the transmission chain.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.52 The Committee is concerned at the low number of Tests per Million population in States 
such as Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal etc. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the State Governments to shed their lackadaisical approach and continue 
tracking, testing and isolating so that Covid cases do not spike in the winter months. 
  (Para 3.50) 
Action Taken 

73 
 
3.53 MoHFW has been following up with these States on a regular basis through video 
conferencing and formal communications, with particular reference to increase quantum of 
testing by ensure optimum utilization of laboratory capacities, keeping confirmation percentage 
below 5%, use of RT-PCR and rapid antigen-based testing as per ICMR protocols. 
Over the period (September to Decembe r), all these States showed a decline in trajectory of 
COVID-19 cases and deaths. The trajectory of COVID -19 cases in the country however 
registered a resurgence from February 2021 onwards. 
Further Recommendation  
3.54 The Committee observes that the North-East region was engulfed during the second 
wave of the pandemic Covid-19. The Committee’s apprehension  came true as whatever 
efforts authorities  took to prevent spread of the pandemic  proved inadequate . T he 
Committee believes that it's high time Ministry pulls up its socks and takes concrete steps 
to improve the largely insufficient  healthcare facilities in the North-East Region of the 
country.  
3.55 The Ministry should ensure that its guidelines and advisories  regarding Covid 
Appropriate Behaviour (CAB) are strictly implemented in letter and spirit.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.56 The Committee underlines the need of biosafety to protect the world community from any 
activity signaling bioterrorism. The adverse effects of Covid -19 pandemic have taught the lesson 
on the importance of controlling biological agents and the need of strategic partnerships among 
different nations. The Committee, therefore, feels that the present time is the most appropriate 
for the Government to formulate  effective laws to counter bioterrorism. The Committee also 
believes with expanding network of VRDLs, ICMR would serve as an important platform for 
diagnosis and surveillance of existing as well as emerging viral infections and thus make the 
country bio-secured against life threatening viruses and the menace of bioterrorism. 
                            (Para 3.52) 
Action Taken

through the following actions: 
 Training/re-training of VRDLs in biosafety and biosecurity. 
 Setting up new BSL-3 facilities in ICMR institutes / VRDLs 
3.58 Laying down guidelines for construction and validation of BSL-3 labs. 
Further Recommendation

at least one BSL -3 lab in each VRDL spread across different S tates of the country.  The

Report for establishing at least one BSL -4 lab in each zone/ region viz. North, East, West, 

74 
 
Central and South. The Committee hopes that the Government would ensure fast -track 
establishment of both BSL-3 and BSL-4 labs within a fixed timeline. The Government must

Observation/Recommendation 
3.60 The Committee expresses concern over inadequate investment on public health research 
even though innovation play pivotal role in controlling the sp read of disease. The country lacks 
resilient field surveillance to detect potential cluster of diseases. Lack of investment leads to 
dependence on imports of diagnostic kits and development of vaccine and drugs which ultimately 
enhances 'out of pocket expe nditure' of common populace. The Committee strongly recommends 
the higher investment on research and development and innovation in the field of health research 
at multiple levels to contain zoonotic virals like COVID -19 and to establish One Health 
Surveillance System with potential warning system of microbial spill over. The Committee is 
distressed to note the recent UIS data (UNESCO Institute of Statistics data) expressing that India 
invests only 0.65 percent of GDP on Research and Development. India's GER D as a percentage 
of GDP was 0.67 in 2017 and 0.65 in 2018. The Gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD) as 
a percentage of GDP is the total intramural expenditure on R&D performed in the national 
territory during a specific reference period expressed as a  percentage of GDP of the national 
territory. The Committee notes that India's GERD is well below the world average and the 
GERD of other countries. Countries like United States of America spend almost 2.84 percent of 
its GDP on research whereas China also  spends 2.19 percent of its GDP on research. The 
Committee deprecates the fact that India's lower appropriation on Research speaks volumes of 
how neglected the R&D sector has been in the country. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends that the Minis try should at least increase its spending on research to the world 
average of 1.72 as a percentage of GDP within two years. The Committee also recommends the 
Ministry to set specific expenditure targets for R&D and for promotion of science, technology 
and innovation (STI). This dedicated separate budgetary allocation should be supported even in 
financial crisis situations so that research activities do not suffer in the wake of any unforeseen 
circumstances. 
                            (Para 3.64)

COVID Management under Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY Scheme 
Observation/Recommendation 
3.66 The Committee notes that NHA has introduced a process of temporary empanelment for 
the hospitals to avail benefits of Ayushman Bharat Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM -JAY) through 
HEM Lite. The Committee welcomes such an initiative considering the gross shortage of 
adequate healthcare facilities. However, the Committee recommends the Ministry to effectively 
scrutinize the whole procedure of temporary empanellement of hospitals so that instances of 
fraudulent healthcare behaviour are avoided. The Committee also recommen ds the Ministry to 
empanel more hospitals especially in areas and States with weak health infrastructure to ensure 
continued supply of essential healthcare services. 
                             (Para 4.14) 
Action Taken 
3.67 The temporary empanelment process using HEM Lite was a special measure in view of 
pandemic-induced circumstances and has ceased to operate now. A total of 535 applications (all 
private) were received under HEM lite module. Out of these, 141 hospitals were empanelled. 
Further, all these hospitals are being moved to draft mode under regular empanelment module. In 
draft mode these hospitals cannot raise fresh pre -authorization request. Standard operating 
procedure will be followed for regularizing their empane lment. For empaneling more hospitals, 
following steps have been taken:   
 All eligible public hospitals including those under the administrative jurisdiction of 
Central Government ministries have been empaneled.   
 A roadmap is being prepared for empaneling majority 100 bed hospitals under the 
scheme. 
 Prominent corporate hospital chains are being approached for empanelment under the 
scheme. In this direction, State Health Agencies have been asked to engage with non -
empaneled hospitals . 

77 
 
 National Health Author ity (NHA) and State  Health Agencies (SHAs) are regularly 
organizing meetings of national and local chapters of Indian Medical Association to seek 
their support in augmenting the role of private healthcare providers . 
  Special incentive over and above the package cost is being provided to NABH accredited 
hospitals.  
3.68 Additionally, a 10% incentive is being given to hospital empaneled in Aspirational 
Districts. This is aimed at attracting investment by private sector in such underserved areas. 
3.69 So far, 24,137 hospitals (including public and private) are empaneled under the scheme. 
Further Recommendation 
3.70 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry  in terms of attracting 
investment by private sector in underserved areas . The Committee desires to know 
whether any assessment has been made with respect  to identifying such areas and S tates 
which need urgent assistance to strengthen their health infrastructure  and incorporating 
the targeted beneficiaries within the ambit of the  Scheme. The Committee seeks to know 
number of hospitals empanelled in the rural areas out of the 141 empanelled hospitals. The 
Committee recommends that more hospitals having facilities to provide emergency services 
arising out of pandemics like Covid -19 should be empanelled in the rural  areas of the 
country.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.71 The Committee is disappointed to note that many poor people have not been included 
under the scheme due to old SECC data and there is no provision to even update or revise the 
list of beneficiaries. The Committee is not convinced by the argument that State  Governments 
can add beneficiaries at their own cost under State schemes. The Committee believes that States 
generally are fund -starved and it would not be appropriate to lay additional burden on them. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry  and NHA must re -visit the idea of 
revising and updating the list of beneficiaries and not deprive poor strata of society who should 
be given coverage under the scheme. 
                             (Para 4.20) 
Action Taken 
3.72 The beneficiary database under AB-PMJAY has been frozen as per the approval of the 
cabinet and currently there is no mechanism to include additional beneficiaries. The possibility 
of using National Food Security Act (NFSA) data for rationalization and expansion of 
beneficiary base under PMJAY is being explored in consultation with all the stakeholders. Also, 
IT platform, Health Benefit Packages, Empanelled Healthcare providers of PMJAY can also be 
used by other health protection schemes for poor families who may not have figured in  the 
original database. With this in view, National Health Authority (NHA) is actively consulting 
with other Ministries and Departments implementing social security schemes in the country. 
Further Recommendation 

78 
 
3.73 The Committee  fails to comprehend the r ationale behind freez ing the beneficiary 
database and thus depriving the deserving large chunk of poor people from availing the 
benefits of AB -PMJAY, especially in rural areas. The Committee understands that t he 
objective of the scheme can only be fully re alized if the poor people who actually need the 
benefits are enrolled in this scheme at the earliest. The Committee strongly recommends 
the NHA (National Health Authority)  to expand the beneficiary base under the scheme in 
consultation with other Ministries/Departments implementing other social security schemes 
in the country.  
Observation/Recommendation 
3.74 The Committee is of the view that engagement of both private and public sector is a must 
for ensuring robust delivery of healthcare services under the  Scheme ABPMJAY. The Committee 
understands that Covid treatment rate and charges for other health package for small private 
hospitals may not be sustainable which would discourage private hospitals from empanelling 
under the Scheme. The Committee therefore  recommended the Ministry to rationalize the 
package rates especially in rural areas where people suffer due to a weak primary healthcare 
infrastructure. 
                             (Para 4.29) 
Action Taken 
3.75 Revision of benefit packages listed under AB-PMJAY is a continuous process based on 
feedback received from respective stakeholders. NHA has a dedicated medical cell which is 
consulted for technical inputs. The inputs of the medical cell are then put up to the respective 
review committee. Post that  States are consulted for understanding their views. Finally, the 
inputs are provided to the NHA Governing Board for making a decision. Further, State 
Governments have been given flexibility to increase the costs of health benefit packages within 
certain band to cater to temporal and spatial variations While NHA devised a national package 
for COVID treatment, flexibility was given to States to modify the package rates for COVID 
testing and treatment based on guidelines issued by NHA. 
Further Recommendation 
3.76 The Committee firmly believes that quality healthcare facilities in the rural areas 
can be developed by encouraging the participation of  the private sector in the development 
of healthcare systems. The Committee , therefore, reiterates its recommendation for 
engaging both private and public sector for ensuring robust delivery of healthcare services 
under the Scheme Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY).

ADMINISTRATIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOCKDOWN & UNLOCKING 
 In view of the loss of life during the second wave of the Covid -19 pandemic, the 
Committee believes that the measures taken by the Ministry to contain/prevent spread of 
SARS-COV-2 proved to be squarely inadequate. The Committee believes that focus should 
be on strengthening of health infrastructure, ensuring adequate availability of beds, 
adequate supply of oxygen cylinders and essential medicines etc. Besides, the Government 
must aggressively keep pushing the vaccination programme in terms of granting appr oval 
to more vaccines, ramping up vaccines’ production, enhancing delivery capacity and 
increasing the vaccination rate.  
(Para 3.5) 
 With the incidence of highly mutated Omicron (B.1.1.529) strain of Covid virus, the 
Committee strongly believes that the efficacy of the vaccines must be evaluated. The 
concerns with regards to the new strain developing immunoescape mechanism need to be 
critically addressed. The Committee apprehends that rise in mutations in the virus may 
lead to reporting of more virulent and transmissible strain of Covid virus in the country. 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to adopt Zero Toleran ce 
Covid-19 Policy and closely track Covid cases across the country.  
(Para 3.6) 
CONTINGENCY PLAN 
The Committee believes that timely detection and isolation of potentially infectious 
people is very crucial in reducing the impact of the pandemic Covid -19. The importance of 
diagnostic testing therefore, cannot be overlooked. An efficient and widely deployed testing 
mechanism will go a long way in preventing the spread of the infection. The Committee is 
pained to note that although the second wave came almost six months after the peak of the 
first wave, India’s testing infrastructure remained abysmal and highly insufficient. The 
Committee is of the opinion that to combat current pandemic Covid -19 and other future 
emergencies, India must realise its full testing  capacity and augment’s this capacity even 
further. The government should ensure that the testing should far outpace the growth of 
the cases to arrest future waves of Covid-19 early.  
 (Para 3.11) 
 The Committee also notes that with the new strain of Covid, Omicron (B.1.1.529) 
exhibiting 30+ mutations, tracking and testing facilities especially at airports must also be 
strengthened and rigorous testing and screening of travelers must be carried out. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to explore imposing travel restrictions and 
isolating passengers from 'at -risk' countries, as part of their new covid strain containment 
strategy. With WHO designating Omicorn as "Variant of Concern", the Governme nt must 
take immediate measures to prevent the transmission of any newer strains in the country.  
(Para 3.12)

Service' (IHS) in the Center and across States as a dedicated, effi cient, and adequately

resourced public health cadre on the pattern of Indian Administrative Service (IAS). It also

network of ASHAs, ANMs and other community health workers and the necessary support

 The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s efforts in spreading the network of 
Viral Research & Diagnostics Laboratories, Multi - Disciplinary Research Units and Modal 
Rural Health Research Units in the country. I t however strongly believes that 
incorporating modern technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) as positive intervention 
in these initiatives can bear rich dividends in terms of quality, delivery and cost 
optimization of healthcare delivery services. Therefore, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministry must increase funding for machine learning and 
artificial intelligence-based projects and encourage the development of AI based systems, 
methods and tools in healthcare.  
(Para 3.65) 
 
 

97 
 
COVID MANAGEMENT UNDER AYUSHMAN BHARAT-PMJAY SCHEME 
 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry in terms of attracting 
investment by private sector in underserved areas. The Committee desires to know 
whether any assessment has been made with r espect to identifying such areas and States 
which need urgent assistance to strengthen their health infrastructure and incorporating 
the targeted beneficiaries within the ambit of the Scheme. The Committee seeks to know 
number of hospitals empanelled in the rural areas out of the 141 empanelled hospitals. The 
Committee recommends that more hospitals having facilities to provide emergency services 
arising out of pandemics like Covid -19 should be empanelled in the rural areas of the 
country.  
(Para 3.70)  
 The Committee fails to comprehend the rationale behind freezing the beneficiary 
database and thus depriving the deserving large chunk of poor people from availing the 
benefits of AB -PMJAY, especially in rural areas. The Committee understands that the 
objective of the scheme can only be fully realized if the poor people who actually need the 
benefits are enrolled in this scheme at the earliest. The Committee strongly recommends 
the NHA (National Health Authority) to expand the beneficiary base under the scheme  in 
consultation with other Ministries/Departments implementing other social security schemes 
in the country.  
(Para 3.73) 
 The Committee firmly believes that quality healthcare facilities in the rural areas 
can be developed by encouraging the participatio n of the private sector in the development 
of healthcare systems. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation for 
engaging both private and public sector for ensuring robust delivery of healthcare services 
under the Scheme Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY). 
(Para 3.76) 
COVID MANAGEMENT THROUGH AYUSH SYSTEM 
 The Committee acknowledges the research work being carried out by various 
organizations under the wings of the Ministry of AYUSH. However, the Committee 
believes tha t more needs to be done to equip the traditional systems of medicine with 
scientific base grounded on in -depth research. The Committee desires that AYUSH 
research work carried out by the institutes aimed towards recording and publishing the 
detailed process of extracting the active ingredient from herbs/plants, its effect initially in 
cell models, then in animals, and finally human trials. To facilitate transition from 
alternative systems to mainstream systems of medicine, it is all the more necessary to bu ild, 
promote and sustain this evidence based framework for the practitioners of the traditional 
systems.  
(Para 3.90) 
The Committee notes the wide range of research studies going on in AYUSH 
research Councils with respect to management of Covid -19, however, the Committee finds 
that the Ministry of AYUSH has not given any justification for delay in approvals for 
clinical and population based research studies. The Committee reiterates its 

98 
 
recommendation seeking clear guidelines with respect to research studie s along with 
proper timelines for the approval process. The Committee would also like to emphasize 
that the outcome of all these research studies especially related to the Covid -19 must be 
recorded, published and adequately placed in the public domain. The  Committee may also 
be apprised of AYUSH research outcomes highlighting concrete evidence in management 
of Covid-19.  
(Para 3.113) 
 The Committee recommends to evolve stringent regulatory framework to tackle the 
problems of failed samples and ensure qualit y control of AYUSH drugs. Strict and 
exemplary action in a time bound manner must be taken against those who are involved in 
manufacturing of spurious/low quality AYUSH drugs. The Committee expects the Ministry 
to fix the responsibility of the officials co ncerned who approve low/substandard quality 
drugs. The Committee wishes to be informed about the action taken by the responsible 
authorities in dealing with the misleading advertisements and unwarranted claims about 
drugs and other solutions in the last th ree years. The Committee is of the view that it is 
high time to effect amendments in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs and 
Magic Remedies Act 1954 to make the provisions relating to offences and penalties/ 
stringent and effective enough to contro l and contain the misleading advertisements, poor 
quality products, cases of adverse reactions, etc.  
(Para 3.116) 
 The Committee is disappointed to observe that the Ministry of AYUSH is silent on 
its recommendation requiring a dedicated AYUSH Covid Care C entre in all the states. The 
Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry should undertake concrete steps to 
popularize the Indian systems of medicine to complement the modern system of medicine 
in management of Covid -19. The Committee strongly de sires the Ministry to contemplate 
on this and apprises the Committee in this regard.  
(Para 3.119) 
The Committee emphasizes that the major roadblock in delivering the quality 
healthcare services is insufficient public health spending. Needless to say, unless the 
government sets aside sufficient funds for healthcare, the prevailing state of public health  
care systems cannot be improved. Inadequate public spending increases Out of Pocket 
expenditure owing to irrational pricing of life saving equipments, drugs etc, as was evident 
in the second wave of pandemic Covid -19. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
expenditure in healthcare must be enhanced adequately to ensure liquidity and cash flow 
availability. This will help ease out financial distress in healthcare and infrastructure and 
as a result the medium sized hospitals and nursing homes can cont ribute in managing the 
health emergencies.  
(Para 3.123) 
 The Committee further recommends the Government to evolve a mechanism to 
regulate the pricing of life saving drugs, particularly during emergencies and its effective 
implementation.  
(Para 3.124) 

99 
 
 The Committee expects Government to ensure that education facilities for students 
particularly of economically weaker sections do not suffer further due to future Covid -19 
waves. The Committee takes note of growing public debate over re -opening of schools. The 
Committee may be apprised of whether the Ministry has done any studies regarding 
various age-group of students with respect to their immune response, mental health, ability 
to practice social distancing norms and other critical parameters affecting th eir health 
before allowing reopening of schools. The Committee notes that physical and mental health 
of children has been the area of concern during pandemic Covid -19.  The Committee 
maybe apprised of studies carried out on impact of online classes, absenc e of classroom 
schooling on overall development of children.  
(Para 3.127) 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry had projected an amount of Rs. 5435.55 
crore in BE 2021 -22 for promoting various Schemes in AYUSH sector to which the  
Ministry of Finance all ocated an amount of Rs.2970.30 crore for the year 2021 -22 which is 
39.97 per cent more than the allocation made in 2020 -21. The Committee believes that the 
Ministry of AYUSH is capable of absorbing more funds under its different schemes. The 
Committee, therefore recommends that the Ministry of AYUSH should plead for increased 
allocation from the Ministry of Finance in the ensuing financial years.  
(Para 3.131)

and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Thirty -First Report of the Committee on Action Ta ken by

Report on Demands for Grants 2021-22 (Demand No. 4) of the Ministry of AYUSH.

II.    MACRO ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
Recommendation 
1.8 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the sharp shortfall in allocation of the 
Ministry as compared to the projected demand, despite its repeated recommendation for 
increasing the budgetary allocation of the Ministry, keeping in view the scope, reach and value 
AYUSH can add to the health of the people. Given its indigenous/traditional element, cost 
effectiveness and a safe alternative to modern system of medicine, the Ministry of AY USH, 
through its schemes and strategies, can help AYUSH system of healthcare to emerge as a 
valuable system of medicine in healthcare delivery. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that 
budgetary constraints should not be allowed to act as a stumbling block to achieve the mission 
objectives to position AYUSH system as the primary and preferred system of healthcare in India. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate budgetary support be provided to the 
Ministry as and when required by it. 
(Para 2.3) 
Action Taken 
1.9 The Concerns of the Committee has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance, vide 
Secretary (AYUSH)‘s D.O. letter No.H -11013/9/2021-Budget dated29.04.2021  for providing 
adequate budgetary support to this Ministry.

Recommendation 
1.16 The Committee observes that the allocation for Ministry of AYUSH is 4.17% of the 
Health Budget as against 3.26% of the Health Budget in 2020-21 and the increase witnessed this 
year is negligible. The Committee has been recommending, time and again, that at least 5% of 
the total Health Budget should be earmarked for Ministry of AYUSH. Thou gh the percentage of 
allocation to the Ministry of AYUSH in comparison to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
has marginally improved and crossed 4 percent mark but this is not adequate. To establish 
Ayush as an effective alternative system of medicine, budgetary resources will have to be 
comparatively increased to provide a level playing field. The Committee believes that AYUSH 
systems of medicine are the treasure of country’s traditional knowledge systems which need to be 
re-discovered and promoted. At a time, when the whole world is dealing with pandemic Covid -
19, the vital role of Indian Systems of Medicine owing to their effective prophylactic usage 
cannot be underestimated. Needless to say, the AYUSH Systems are integrative and economical 
systems of medicine which need financial support so as to tap its full potential and proliferation 
at Panchayatlevel. The Committee, accordingly, reiterates its earlier recommendation of 
increasing budget of AYUSH Ministry to at least 5% of the budget of Health Minis try at the RE 
stage 2021 -22 itself. The Committee desires that the Ministry of Finance may consider to 
allocate 10% of the Health Budget to Ministry of AYUSH from the next financial year 
henceforth. 
(Para 2.19)

1.77 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must ensure stringent implementation 
of Pharmacovigilance schemes. For th is, the Committee recommends that the education -related 
to Pharmacovigilance should be included in the curriculum itself and periodic awareness 
programmes should be organized for both health care professionals and patients. Moreover, 
monthly reporting of A DRs (Adverse Drug Reactions) reports should be made mandatory at all 
AYUSH wellness centres. The Committee believes that maintaining a comprehensive and 
updated medicine literature database would provide credible and latest medical information to

regulatory action. The Committee desires that the submission of Periodic Safety  Update Reports 
(PSUR) must be made mandatory for AYUSH drugs. The Committee, therefore, would like to 
reiterate that all these measures can only be realized if the Pharmacovigilance network is

Pharmacovigilance Program of ASU & H drug since December 2017. Through this scheme a

Recommendation 
3.91 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives taken by the Ministry of AYUSH through its 
various institutes in mainstreaming AYUSH systems of medicine. However, the Committee is of 
the opinion that the maj ority of the work done is preventive in nature and recommends that the

shows etc. to bring some tangible progress in the adoption of Indian traditional systems. The 
Committee notes the main reason behind the poor export of Indian traditiona l drugs is their 
failure to meet global norms on safety and efficacy. The Committee also notes that licensing of

Further Recommendation 
3.119 The Committee takes into account the significant R&D and public health initiatives 
undertaken by various C ouncils of AYUSH to harness the potential of AYUSH systems.  
The Committee appreciates that c ollaborative research studies with different countries 
would help in establishing the system as the credible and scientific system of medicine 
which may emerge as a curative alternative to modern medicines.   The Committee, 
however, is disappointed to note that the Ministry has not given any information about 
reasons for poor export of ASU&H drugs. The Commit tee's concerns about ASU drugs 
failing to meet global norms on safety and efficacy have not been addresse d.  The 
Committee is also surprised that the Ministry has not paid attention to the point 
highlighted by it regarding lack of uniformity in the approac h of different States with 
respect to ASU Drugs as Health is a State subject.  The Committee emphasise s that given 
the increasing popularity of AYUSH systems especially during pandemic Covid -19, it is 
high time to showcase the effectiveness of ASU&H drugs in domestic market as well as 
global arena . The Committee recommends the Ministry to have a standard licensing 
process based on uniform parameters across all the States so that the drug formulations do 
not vary in different States and also conform to global norms of safety and efficacy. This 

65 
 
would go a long way in establishing Indian System of Medicine as an alternative system  of 
medicine.  
 
Recommendation 
3.120 The Committee believes that misleading and unfounded advertisements particularly by 
ASU drug makers will force people to gradually desist from consuming such ASU formulations. 
The Committee recommends that provisions of both the Drugs & Cosmetics Act Rules & Magical 
Remedies Act should be made more stringent to tackle the problem of misleading and unfounded 
advertisements. The Committee desires the Ministry to revisit both the period of imprisonment 
and the fine amount under these rules to regulate and cont rol the violation of the provisions of 
the said Acts. The licensing authorities and drug controllers at the State level must also take 
prompt actions against any such misconduct.  
(Para 4.11)

3.122 The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry has not paid attention to the 
area of concern regarding lack of prompt action in response to misleading and unfounded 
advertisements about AYUSH drugs/products. The Committee had recommended for

authorities and State Drug Controllers should have adequate powers to take prompt and

Recommendation 
3.123 The Committee observes that the trend of dis eases as well as severity of illnesses has 
undergone a substantial change in the modern age. Advancement in modern science has brought 
out a revolution in the way one identifies, diagnoses and treats illnesses now -a-days. The 
Committee believes that AYUSH with its traditional/classic knowledge has immense potential in 
devising a holistic approach against the ever changing challenges in the health sector and 
ensuring good health of the masses. However, AYUSH has remained neglected and modern 
system of medicine, with a scientific evidence base, has overshadowed AYUSH's popularity and 
growth. Nevertheless, the Committee observes that with the formation of a separate Ministry for 
AYUSH, various efforts have been made for the revival of AYUSH over the years. The Committee 
appreciates the Schemes and Programmes implemented by the Ministry of AYUSH for 
mainstreaming of AYUSH services and acknowledges its satisfactory trend of budgetary 
utilization. The Committee also believes that it is high time to make AYUSH more competitive 
and expand its outreach across States as well as in the international market. The Committee 
believes that for strengthening AYUSH research, education institutes, its industry and the quality 
of AYUSH healthcare, a substantial enhancement in budgetary allocation is the need of the hour. 
AYUSH must also collaborate and coordinate with other scientific disciplines as well as the 
modern system of medicine. Integration of AYUSH with modern advances will enhance its 
reliability and scientifically validate the ancient AYUSH traditions. 
(Para 4.30)

Covid-19 mitigation management. The Committee desires that AIIA needs to popularize 
AYURAKSHA project amongst common masses for attracting more and more people 
towards A yush system. The Committee believes that the clinical studies of CCRAS, 
intending to scientifically validate the efficacy and safety of classical Ayurvedic 
formulations to generate tangible evidence would not only yield in scientifically validated 
new drug  development but would also instill public faith in quality assured Ayurvedic 
treatment. The Committee, therefore, recommends that CCRAS should adopt a targeted 
approach and chalk out an action plan to achieve the same.  
(Para 3.15)  
 The Committee is of t he opinion that merely by writing to States Governments to 
check the practice of AYUSH System by quacks, the Ministry of AYUSH should not 
absolve itself of its responsibility to stop this menace as it not only brings disrepute to the 
AYUSH system of medici ne but also discourages people to have trust in this system. The 
Ministry, therefore, must think of devising certain code under which stern legal action 
could be taken against the quacks. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of 
Health & Family W elfare must examine and consider the regulatory amendments under 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1947 as suggested by the Ministry of AYUSH without delay to 
improve the quality, efficacy and safety of ASU drugs. The Ministry of AYUSH must take 
up this matter with  the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare on priority basis and inform 
the Committee on the action taken on the matter. 
(Para 3.17)  
 

73 
 
MACRO ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 The Committee takes note of the status of construction of the projects of National 
Institutes and finds that except for National Institute of Homoeopathy, Phase -II, Kolkata, 
all the Institutes are lagging behind with respect to their physical and financial progress. 
The Committee understands that given the prevailing pandemic Covid -19 si tuation, it is 
but natural that the deadline for physical completion of construction work at all Institutes 
would certainly not be met.  The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry must 
make all out efforts to complete the ongoing projects at the earliest so that all the institutes 
could be made operational for the benefit of the people. 
(Para 3.22)  
 
 The Committee is disappointed to note that as of now, 20 -23 States/UT 
Governments have submitted their State Annual Action Plans ( SAAP), 2 States/UT  
Governments have submitted UCs through the NAM web portal and the remaining 
States/UTs are under process.  The Committee apprehends that the NAM web portal is not 
popular amongst States/UTs for prompt submission of UCs despite imparting necessary 
training to officials of States/UTs on submission of SAAP, physical and financial report, 
UCs, etc. The Committee is surprised that the States which have submitted their SAAP 
through NAM web portal also have not submitted UCs through the same portal.  The 
Committee believes that such reluctance reeks of evasion of responsibility and 
accountability of funds given.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
persuade all States/UTs to submit not only their SAAP but also pending UCs through the 
web portal. 
(Para 3.25)  
 
SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry of AYUSH in extending the 
co-location of AYUSH facilities at PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals and thus providing 
choice to the patients for different systems of medicines under single window. The 
Committee, however, finds such facilities lacking in Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Daman & Diu and Delhi, etc. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
States/UTs need to be continuously persuaded for sending  proposals through their SAAPS 
for setting up co -location of AYUSH facilities under NHM.  The measures so undertaken 
would not only ensure preferred choice to the patients for different system of medicine 
under single system but also facilitate  mainstreaming of AYUSH services at the grass root 
level.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare would share 
requisite responsibilities in engagement of AYUSH doctors/paramedical staff and their 
training for enhancing the quality of human resource of each AYUSH centre. 
(Para 3.28)  
 
 The Committee expresses its concern that only 835 AYUSH HWCs against the 
target of 4436 HWCs could be made functional in 12 States which indicates the inadequacy 

74 
 
of steps taken by the Ministry.  The Committee i s utterly disappointed to note such tardy 
progress in operationalisation of HWCs. The Committee underlines the need of a 
streamlined procedure to ensure the completion of setting up of AYUSH HWCs within a 
specified time with adequate manpower and infrastru cture and provision of operational 
cost. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to engage the remaining States/UTs 
which have not yet started the process of making AYUSH HWCs functional so that 
equitable distribution of AYUSH HWCs, keeping in view the geographical extent and 
population of States/UTs, is assured.    
(Para 3.31)  
 The Committee is not convinced with the response and justification given by the 
Ministry on the mismatch between the target of setting up of AYUSH HWCs and actual 
operationalisation during a stipulated time frame.  The Committee, in this connection, 
reiterates its recommendation made in para 3.16 that a demarcation in physical targets 
with respect to approval of HWCs and targets for its operationalisation needs to be clearly 
spelt out.  The Committee recommends that a realistic timeline must be determined to 
make HWCs functional with requisite infrastructure and human resource. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry should work in tandem with States/UTs 
Governments on the operationalisation of all the approved HWCs. The Committee believes 
that proper monitoring and field visits will be of immense help in expediting the 
operationalisation process of HWCs.  
(Para 3.34)  
 The Committee is disappointed that the  Ministry has not shared any information 
about its effort undertaken to tap the full potential of the North East Regions with respect 
to the rich biodiversity in the NER.  The Committee firmly believes that NER with its rich 
bio-diversity and region specif ic plants of medicinal values must be focused upon for 
exploration, collection, documentation for sustainable and optimal utilization of medicinal 
plants.  The Committee, accordingly, reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must 
focus on North East  Regions and also liaise with Ministry of Environment and Forests for 
conservation and maintenance of potential utilization of hubs and medicinal plants. 
(Para 3.39)  
   The Committee acknowledges the efforts put in by the Ministry for encouraging 
farmers to cultivate medicinal plants. However, the Ministry has  not been able to take this 
scheme to the length and breadth of the country as a result of which majority of farmers 
are deprived of its benefits.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates is recommendat ion to 
make the presence of this scheme felt throughout the country in a time bound manner.  
(Para 3.42)  
The Committee takes into account that although it is mandatory for all Ayurvedic 
medicine manufacturers to comply with the standards prescribed under Ayurvedic 
Pharmacopeia of India (API) which includes Pharmacopeial standards for heavy metals 
content, microbiological limits, aflatoxines, etc., it is, however, skeptical about the 
adherence to these prescribed standards in the absence of proper monitorin g and 
supervision.  The Committee, time and again, has been emphasizing upon quality control of 
ASU&H drugs with the purpose of popularizing its domestic use and global acceptance.  

75 
 
The Committee hopes that all components of the new scheme outlined for the  duration of 
15th Finance Commission would be implemented effectively to strengthen the whole regime 
of standardization, scientific validation, Pharmacovigilance, etc.  The Committee reiterates 
its recommendation regarding increasing the credibility of AYU SH system to meet 
scientific global scrutiny and scientific validation of new Ayush drugs development 
including pre-clinical and clinical trials to showcase its evidence based products.     
(Para 3.44)  
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the rec ruitment process for filling up 
of 09 posts regulatory posts for creation of a vertical structure in CDSCO is progressing at 
a snail's pace.  The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends that the creation 
of vertical structure for AYUSH under CDS CO should be expedited and the recruitment 
process be completed at the earliest.   
(Para 3.47)  
  The Committee notes that W.H.O Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) has been 
given to 21 Ayurvedic  Drug manufacturers to export their products as per standards and 
other requirements of importing countries. The Committee expects the Ministry to monitor 
whether these 21 manufacturers have in house quality control section and drug testing 
laboratory as p er the schedule 'T' of prescribed Good Manufacturing Practices. The 
Committee would like to be apprised whether any complaints with respect to sub -standard 
or inferior products has/have been received against existing licensed manufacturers in the 
last two years and the action taken against the manufacturers violating the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules, 1945. The Committee, at the same time, recommends the Ministry to 
effectively operationalise the E -Aushadhi portal by activating new application process for 
online registration and license application in order to achieve the set objectives of the 
portal.  
(Para 3.51)  
  The Committee observes that during 2021 -22, an amount to the tune of Rs. 4.10 
crore has been allotted to further strengthen the Pharmacovigilance network and reporting 
mechanism by establishing more peripheral Pharmacovigilance centers i.e. upto 100 by 
ensuring adequate manpower for Pharmacovigilance Centres across the country. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to make an assessment of the operat ional cost of each 
Pharmacovigilance Centre along with the number of workforce required to run it smoothly 
and accordingly project its fund requirement for the scheme.  The Committee recommends 
the Ministry to comply with the findings and observations of t he Comprehensive Impact 
Assessment of the Pharmacovigilance Scheme for its effective execution and actual 
achievement of set objectives on the ground level.  
(Para 3.54)  
 The Committee notes that the various Councils of AYUSH and their institutes are in 
the process of obtaining their NABH accreditation.  The Committee, however, reiterates 
that a timeframe for completing NABH accreditation must be fixed by the Ministry and 
desired the Ministry to keep a close watch to ensure the compliance of NABH standards  by 
those who have been accredited. 
(Para 3.79)  

76 
 
  The Committee is well aware of the grant -in-aid that is given under National 
AYUSH Mission under the component of Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs to State 
ASU&H licensing Authorities/Drug Controllers for technical manpower. The Committee 
wonders that the Ministry is silent on the recommendation of the Committee relating to 
creation of a specialized body for AYUSH Drug Control with requisite expertise at the 
State level on lines of the vertical structure for AYUSH under CDSCO. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to reconsider its recommendation and also explore the 
feasibility of setting up of a specialized body especially for AYUSH Drugs Control at the 
State Level.  
(Para 3.82)  
  The Committee expresses its pleasure that various research institutes are 
undertaking clinical trials for making their research scientific and evidence based.  Such 
clinical trials help to reach a firm conclusion that a par ticular drug is both safe and 
effective.  The Committee is of the considered view that the Indian system of Medicine 
would get a big boost if quality and evidence based scientific research is carried out.  The 
Committee, in this connection, recommends the Ministry to develop a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) in AYUSH systems that would enable researchers to seek 
better ways to utilize each other research outcomes and thus create a platform for sharing 
the database and the experience gained with each other for better R&D outcome.  
(Para 3.90)  
MAINSTREAMING OF AYUSH SYSTEM 
  The Committee takes into account the significant R&D and public health initiatives 
undertaken by various Councils of AYUSH to harness the potential of AYUSH systems.  
The C ommittee appreciates that collaborative research studies with different countries 
would help in establishing the system as the credible and scientific system of medicine 
which may emerge as a curative alternative to modern medicines.  The Committee, 
however, is disappointed to note that the Ministry has not given any information about 
reasons for poor export of ASU&H drugs. The Committee's concerns about ASU drugs 
failing to meet global norms on safety and efficacy have not been addressed.  The 
Committee is  also surprised that the Ministry has not paid attention to the point 
highlighted by it regarding lack of uniformity in the approach of different States with 
respect to ASU Drugs as Health is a State subject.  The Committee emphasises that given 
the increa sing popularity of AYUSH systems especially during pandemic Covid -19, it is 
high time to showcase the effectiveness of ASU&H drugs in domestic market as well as 
global arena. The Committee recommends the Ministry to have a standard licensing 
process based on uniform parameters across all the States so that the drug formulations do 
not vary in different States and also conform to global norms of safety and efficacy. This 
would go a long way in establishing Indian System of Medicine as an alternative system o f 
medicine.  
(Para 3.119)  
  The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry has not paid attention to the 
area of concern regarding lack of prompt action in response to misleading and unfounded 
advertisements about AYUSH drugs/products. The Committ ee had recommended for 

77 
 
making the provisions of both Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Magical Remedies Act stricter 
so as to dissuade drugs manufacturers from giving misleading advertisement about 
AYUSH products.  The Committee, in this connection, reiterates t hat the licensing 
authorities and State Drug Controllers should have adequate powers to take prompt and 
stern action against such misconduct under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Magical 
Remedies Act. The Committee further recommends the Ministry to come u p with 
appropriate amendments in the concerned legislations accordingly.  
(Para 3.122)  
 The Committee appreciates the various initiatives of the Ministry of AYUSH to 
promote and develop Indian system of Medicine.  Given the vast potential of Indian System 
of Medicine in contemporary times and especially during pandemic Covid -19, the 
Committee believes that Indian System of Medicine has huge capacity to position itself as 
an effective and economical system of medicine as an alternative to modern system of 
medicine. This will help reduce out of pocket expenditure on health.  The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to identify the 'Key Concern Areas' especially with regard to 
quality of education and research, drugs and overall healthcare delivery systems in 
AYUSH institutions. The Committee recognizes the importance of collaborative researches 
as well as clinical trials for better research outcomes. Since Ayurveda is the valued heritage 
of the glorious past of our country, it needs proper propagation at the grass-root and global 
level. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the Ministry to lay sp ecial focus on the 
regulation and control over safety and efficacy of Ayurveda drugs and products to enable 
the market of the AYUSH products grow internationally and stand to any scientific 
scrutiny.  Keeping in view the vast arena of AYUSH systems, the Co mmittee recommends 
the Ministry to chalk out specific course of action to combat the challenges ahead for 
strengthening the infrastructure, education and practice of AYUSH systems and expand 
the reach of these systems across the country and abroad.  
(Para 3.126)
